tagline: A lake loop joins stone waysides with the Mille Lacs Band’s story.
intro: The Lake Mille Lacs Scenic Byway circles the lake on 68 paved miles, with lake views and communities along the way. The byway organization allows 1.5 to 2 hours for the drive. Explore Minnesota identifies it as the state’s 22nd byway and highlights wildlife viewing, state parks, Civilian Conservation Corps sites and the Mille Lacs Indian Museum and Trading Post.

The western shore’s motoring history began before this loop: a scenic highway was designated there in 1917, and the road became U.S. 169 in 1931. During the Depression, the Minnesota Highway Department used New Deal funds and labor to realign roads and create waysides for motorists. Civilian Conservation Corps workers built the Garrison Concourse between 1936 and 1939, part of a larger lakeshore parkway project. Near Garrison, the same camp widened ten miles of highway from two lanes to four and built four stone-faced bridges. The work fell short of the original ambition for a scenic highway all the way round the lake.

From Isle, head southwest through Wahkon toward Onamia, then north past Vineland to Garrison on the northwest shore. The loop uses Highways 27, 169, 18 and 47, plus Shakopee Lake Road. Continue along the north shore through Wealthwood to Malmo, then follow the east shore south to Isle.

moments.title: Mille Lacs Kathio State Park
moments.text: Nineteen identified archaeological sites lie within Mille Lacs Kathio State Park. The earliest dates to the Archaic period and contains evidence of copper tool manufacture. Preserved habitation sites and mound groups document Dakota culture and Ojibwe-Dakota relationships. Later, logging changed the landscape: trees felled over the half-century after the 1850s were floated down the Rum River or across Mille Lacs Lake to sawmills. The Kathio Historic District became a National Historic Landmark in 1964. The park also has an observation tower to climb, with hiking, biking and camping among its other visitor activities.

moments.title: Mille Lacs Indian Museum and Trading Post
moments.text: The Four Seasons Room follows an Ojibwe year through life-size dioramas made in 1964. Summer berry picking leads to fall wild ricing, winter hunting and trapping, and a spring maple syrup camp. These are historical representations within a museum devoted to the Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe’s history, culture and contemporary life. Other exhibits display contemporary pow-wow outfits and address sovereignty and self-governance. The present museum opened in 1996, following the original exhibit building’s closure in 1992. Exhibits use both English and Ojibwe, and the collections include bandolier bags, moccasins and birch-bark baskets.

moments.title: Garrison
moments.text: The Garrison Concourse’s roadside overlook projects 160 feet into Mille Lacs Lake. Its D-shaped platform carries a driveway and parking area, with a curving stone walkway along the edge. Civilian Conservation Corps workers began by building a cofferdam to hold back lake water while they laid the wall’s footings. Restoration began in 2011 after ice and waves damaged the wall. Workers recovered several displaced stones from the lakebed and fitted them back into place. The wall’s granite blocks are roughly finished and laid in an irregular pattern. Stone piers punctuate the wall.
moments.notice: Look for the granite-block wall and the stone walkway curving along the lakeward edge.
